CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hypertension and palpitations.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jordan Roberts is a 49-year-old male with a long-standing history of hypertension since young age presenting with resistant hypertension. Patient reports an emergency room visit in March 2026 for elevated blood pressure and palpitations. He attributes this episode to consuming multiple cups of coffee on an empty stomach and believes it was likely a panic attack rather than a true cardiac event. He denies recurrence of palpitations since that time. Patient reports that he thought his blood pressure was improving and was recently started on a new antihypertensive regimen by his new primary care physician approximately one month ago. He is currently monitoring blood pressure daily at home with readings ranging from 146-155 mmHg. He is attempting to reduce his salt intake and exercises by walking on the treadmill when able.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies recurrent palpitations or chest pain. No other acute complaints.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypertension (long-standing, since young age)

MEDICATIONS
Amlodipine 10 mg daily
Benicar HCT (olmesartan/hydrochlorothiazide 40-25 mg) daily (started 1 month ago)
Spironolactone (to be initiated)

ALLERGIES
Not documented

FAMILY HISTORY
Significant for hypertension in multiple family members.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Lives with girlfriend. Exercises by walking on treadmill. Attempting dietary modification with reduced salt intake.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Blood pressure elevated at 146-155 mmHg on home monitoring
General: Alert and oriented
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds normal, no murmurs
Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender on palpation
Extremities: No edema in ankles or feet

RESULTS
Potassium level (1 week prior): 4.0 mEq/L (normal)
Thyroid profile from March 1, 2021: To be copied forward from prior records

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Resistant hypertension on three maxed-out antihypertensive medications. Patient discussed as potentially having resistant hypertension driven by secondary causes such as hyperaldosteronism or parathyroid dysfunction. Plan to add spironolactone to current regimen. Patient counseled on potential side effects including possible dizziness, electrolyte disturbances (hyperkalemia, hyponatremia), and rare side effect of gynecomastia. Emphasized need for adequate hydration and electrolyte monitoring. Patient educated on dietary modifications including DASH diet, salt restriction to less than 2000 mg daily (goal 1500 mg daily), and importance of regular exercise (30 minutes most days can reduce blood pressure by 7-10 points). Directed to heart.org for additional patient education resources. Follow-up appointment scheduled in 2 weeks for blood pressure reassessment and metabolic panel including electrolytes and potassium levels. If inadequate response to spironolactone, patient will be referred to resistant hypertension clinic for evaluation of secondary causes and consideration of procedure-based interventions such as renal denervation. Next medication option if needed would be carvedilol.
